guides.intro: How can an agent pursue the intended goal when rewards, instructions and feedback only describe it imperfectly? This topic follows the gap between measured success and desired behavior, including reward hacking, unintended side effects and goals that fail to generalize.
guides.boundary: Alignment concerns what the agent optimizes. Permissions limit what it can do; monitoring checks what it actually does. These can support alignment without establishing it.
questions: Can a coding agent improve test scores while violating the user’s actual requirements?
Does safe behavior survive changes in tasks, tools and feedback?

readings.why: Organizes accident risks around objectives, supervision and learning; a useful conceptual starting point.
Separates the observed reward from a hidden performance function, making specification failures measurable.

guides.intro: Safe RL learns a useful policy while respecting safety constraints during training and execution. The central design choice is what must be bounded: expected cumulative cost, the probability of failure, or every individual action.
guides.boundary: A bound on expected cost is different from a guarantee that no unsafe action occurs. Check the environment model, constraint definition and assumptions before comparing methods.
questions: Can a policy remain safe when dynamics or constraints change?
How much reward and exploration efficiency are lost for each safety requirement?

readings.why: Introduces constrained policy search with near-constraint satisfaction per iteration under its assumptions.
Uses a synthesized shield to restrict or correct actions against a temporal-logic specification.

guides.intro: This topic asks how a deployment can remain safe when an agent may strategically hide undesirable behavior or subvert its checks. It studies both evidence of deceptive behavior and protocols that limit harm from an untrusted model.
guides.boundary: A constructed deceptive model demonstrates a failure mode; it does not establish how often naturally trained systems deceive. Control protocols should be tested against adaptive attempts to defeat them.
questions: Can the actor and its monitor share the same blind spots?
Which auditing and editing protocols remain useful when the actor knows the defense?

readings.why: Turns intentional subversion into a protocol evaluation problem with trusted and untrusted models.
Constructs persistent backdoors and tests whether safety training removes them.

guides.intro: Agents delegate effort but can also displace human choice. Research here asks when to request approval, how to preserve interruption and correction, and how a person can meaningfully control a long-running task.
guides.boundary: An approval button does not establish meaningful control. The human needs enough information, time and an effective way to change the outcome.
questions: Which irreversible actions require informed approval before execution?
Does an agent preserve the user’s ability to interrupt, revise and revoke delegation?

readings.why: Models incentives to preserve or disable a human off-switch and the role of uncertainty about objectives.
Shows how limited trusted human effort can be allocated within a control protocol.

guides.intro: Oversight evaluates and redirects an agent when a human cannot inspect every step. Assurance organizes evidence for a safety claim. Together they ask who checks the agent, what that checker can observe, and why the resulting evidence should be trusted.
guides.boundary: A strong judge on ordinary tasks may still miss the actor’s failures. Measure correlated errors, audit budgets and performance against deliberate evasion.
questions: What complementary information lets a weaker monitor catch a stronger agent?
Can assurance evidence remain valid after the model or toolchain changes?

readings.why: Proposes debate as a way to help a limited judge assess more complex claims.
Evaluates oversight inside an adversarial deployment protocol rather than only as isolated classification.

guides.intro: Runtime monitoring observes an agent’s trajectory and intervenes before or after risky steps. Monitors may inspect inputs, tool calls, generated code or state changes; the useful unit of analysis is the action sequence and its consequences.
guides.boundary: A detector’s accuracy alone does not describe a deployed monitor. Timing, false alarms, evasion, latency and what happens after an alert all matter.
questions: Can monitoring catch a harmful trajectory before an irreversible action?
How should monitoring trade off false alarms, latency and missed failures?

readings.why: Provides a clear intervention model: inspect proposed actions and enforce a stated safety specification.
Combines input detection, alignment checks and code analysis in an agent guardrail framework.

guides.intro: Formal approaches express a safety property precisely and prove or check it under explicit assumptions. The challenge is connecting the mathematical model to an agent’s changing tools, observations and environment.
guides.boundary: Verified code or a checked rule does not automatically verify the full agent. State which components, transitions and environmental assumptions the guarantee covers.
questions: Can natural-language policies be translated into correct executable constraints?
What happens when the real environment violates the proof assumptions?

readings.why: Connects temporal-logic safety specifications with an executable action shield.
Explores policy reasoning and verification tools for agent trajectories; inspect the scope of each checked claim.

guides.intro: Prompt injection occurs when content that an agent should treat as data influences its instructions or actions. Indirect injection places that content in a webpage, document or tool result the agent encounters while carrying out a legitimate task.
guides.boundary: Distinguish the attacker’s control over external content from the user’s legitimate authority. A successful defense must preserve useful task completion while preventing the attacker’s objective.
questions: Can instruction provenance survive retrieval, summaries, memory and delegated tools?
Do defenses hold under adaptive attacks at the same task utility?

readings.why: An early systematic study of indirect injection through retrieved content and connected applications.
Makes agent utility and adversarial robustness measurable in an extensible tool environment.

guides.intro: Jailbreak research examines attempts to make a model or agent comply with requests that its safety policy should reject. For tool-using agents, the outcome can include a completed sequence of harmful actions rather than only a harmful answer.
guides.boundary: Prompt injection concerns a trust boundary in external content; a jailbreak concerns bypassing behavioral restrictions. They can overlap, but require different attacker models and success criteria.
questions: Does a jailbreak preserve the capabilities needed to finish a harmful multi-step task?
How do refusal behavior and actual tool actions diverge?

readings.why: Establishes an influential automated adversarial-suffix approach; useful background for later agent attacks.
Measures malicious multi-step agent tasks together with retained capability after jailbreaking.

guides.intro: Agents can access private context, retrieve documents and transmit information through tools. This topic studies which data may be used or disclosed, to whom, and under what purpose and consent constraints.
guides.boundary: Training-data extraction, context leakage and unauthorized tool-based exfiltration have different entry points. Identify the sensitive asset and the path that moves it before selecting a defense.
questions: Can an agent enforce purpose limits across multiple tools and recipients?
How can leakage be measured without exposing real private data?

readings.why: Demonstrates extraction of memorized training examples; background for understanding one source of leakage.
Includes private-data exfiltration through tool-integrated agents under indirect injection.

guides.intro: Retrieval and persistent memory give an agent useful context, but can also carry poisoned instructions or false beliefs across tasks. Research follows how content is admitted, retrieved, trusted, updated and forgotten.
guides.boundary: A poisoned document, a corrupted memory and a misleading summary have different persistence and control assumptions. Evaluate effects over later tasks, not only the initial encounter.
questions: Can a single interaction contaminate later decisions after the source disappears?
What evidence is needed to admit, revise or delete a memory?

readings.why: Studies targeted poisoning of an agent’s memory or knowledge base and its retrieval conditions.
Explains why retrieved text can cross the boundary between data and instructions.

guides.intro: An agent depends on models, packages, tool servers, skills and their descriptions. Supply-chain research examines how a compromised dependency or an untrusted update can gain influence over the agent and its environment.
guides.boundary: A protocol implementation is only one part of the chain. Track provenance, versions, trust in providers and changes to permissions; one vulnerable example does not establish the prevalence of a vulnerability.
questions: Can tool descriptions or updates silently change the effective trust boundary?
How can agents verify the origin and intended permissions of third-party skills?

readings.why: An early audit of security issues in connected MCP workflows, useful for defining trust boundaries.
Offers privilege-control mechanisms relevant to limiting the impact of untrusted tools.

guides.intro: Tool safety asks whether an agent’s concrete actions are valid, authorized and safe in context. The research unit includes arguments, execution state, external side effects and recovery after a partially completed action.
guides.boundary: Correct text is insufficient if execution changes the wrong resource. Separate proposed actions, executed actions and observed outcomes, especially for irreversible operations.
questions: How can a system validate risky actions before they affect the real environment?
Can agents recover safely from timeouts, retries and partial completion?

readings.why: Uses an emulated tool sandbox to study difficult-to-stage agent failures and their evaluation.
Organizes diverse interactive environments and failure modes for agent safety evaluation.

guides.intro: This topic asks who an agent is acting for and which operations it may perform. It covers delegated authority, least privilege, access policies and how authorization changes as a task proceeds.
guides.boundary: Authentication identifies a principal; authorization constrains an action. A valid login does not imply permission to use every tool or disclose every accessible item.
questions: Can permissions be bound to a task, recipient and duration?
Does delegation between agents amplify authority beyond the original user’s intent?

readings.why: Makes tool-use privileges explicit and enforces them around an agent’s execution.
Translates guard requests into executable checks, including access-control scenarios.

guides.intro: Embodied agents act through robots or other physical systems, where mistakes can cause collision, injury or damage. Safe learning, perception uncertainty and physical constraints must work together across the control loop.
guides.boundary: A safe plan in a language model does not guarantee safe motion. Distinguish high-level intent, low-level control, sensing assumptions and the simulator-to-reality gap.
questions: Can perception uncertainty be carried into action constraints?
How are safe stops and fallback controllers verified in changing environments?

readings.why: Connects policy optimization to explicit safety constraints, illustrated with simulated robot locomotion.
Shows how action-level enforcement can complement a learned controller under stated assumptions.

guides.intro: Safety can fail through interactions even when individual agents appear competent. This topic studies miscoordination, conflict, collusion, communication attacks and how failures propagate through a network of agents.
guides.boundary: More agents do not automatically provide independent checks. Shared models, information and incentives can create correlated errors or coordinated undesirable behavior.
questions: When does communication improve reliability, and when does it spread a failure?
How can evaluations detect collusion or hidden conflicts of interest?

readings.why: An influential interaction-based oversight proposal; study the judge and incentive assumptions.
Organizes multi-agent risks into miscoordination, conflict and collusion with shared risk factors.

guides.intro: Safety evaluation turns a claim into testable tasks, threat models and outcome measures. A useful evaluation distinguishes failure to complete the legitimate task from unsafe success, and records what its tests leave unexamined.
guides.boundary: Scores from different benchmarks are not directly comparable without matching tasks, attacker access, budgets and model versions. Benchmark coverage does not prove deployment safety.
questions: Do benchmark failures predict failures in long-running real workflows?
How can adaptive attacks, utility and uncertainty be reported together?

readings.why: Makes distinct safety properties measurable in controlled environments.
Pairs legitimate tool tasks with security objectives in an extensible environment.
Provides a broad set of agent environments and failure modes to examine coverage.

guides.intro: Red teaming actively searches for failures under an explicit attacker model. It helps discover cases that a fixed test set misses, but its conclusions depend on attack budgets, allowed access and how successes are checked.
guides.boundary: Failure discovery and prevalence estimation are different tasks. A strong attack demonstrates vulnerability under its conditions; an unsuccessful search is not a general safety guarantee.
questions: Can attack generation avoid sharing the defender’s blind spots?
How do attack success rates change with budget and adaptation?

readings.why: Uses language models to generate test cases for another model, exploring diversity and difficulty.
Offers concrete multi-step malicious tasks for studying agent misuse and jailbreak robustness.

guides.intro: An agent can cause harm without a malicious user or injected instruction. Ambiguous requests, incorrect state estimates, planning mistakes, overconfident tool use and unintended side effects all matter in ordinary workflows.
guides.boundary: Task failure is not always a safety failure, and task success is not always safe. Define the harmful consequence and who bears it, including effects outside the immediate task metric.
questions: Can an agent recognize missing information and ask before taking a risky action?
Which recovery strategies prevent small execution errors from cascading?

readings.why: Frames accident risks from misspecified objectives, limited supervision and distribution shift.
Studies risky tool-use failures in emulated environments, including difficult-to-stage scenarios.
